Recommended read. We are just starting to understand how AI shapes decisions and judgment. At first glance, this might look like a simple, niche passion research project. However, it's an important research direction for understanding where AI's true value emerges and how to optimize agent-human collaboration. If we can better understand when to defer to AI and when expert/human judgment matters, I think this unlocks tremendous value. Yes, it matters for organizations adopting AI, but I see it as an interesting way to better measure human-agent collaboration and discover new, optimal ways to augment collective intelligence. New Anthropic research: How AI agents shape experts' judgment calls When experts delegate work to an agent, do they still make the key decisions? We tested this in a randomized trial with 50 professional data analysts.

Yes, the coding interview is absolutely dead! It should have been gone a long time ago. With coding agents this good, we can now focus on hiring people with high agency, taste, judgment, empathy, and principled thinking. This also gives junior engineers a fair chance. I am often surprised by how better equipped they are, how fast they move, and their creativity and ambition. You need all those qualities in this brave new world. I recently gave a talk at a university, and I suggested to senior students that they look at data (understand and analyze it) and pick a domain they are passionate about. Then build a prototype that tries to solve a problem and share it publicly (X, GitHub, YouTube, Kaggle, etc.). The first project might not get any attention, but if you do this often, you will eventually find someone, or hopefully a few, in the industry who care as much as you do about the problem you are trying to solve. Show that desire and hunger. It matters so much today. If you are just starting your career, don't pay attention to all the noise (e.g., AI taking away jobs, etc.). Keep building and shipping. Master your fundamentals (systems thinking goes a long way today). And stay hungry. The coding interview is dead, at least for my team at Anthropic. I've seen enough to know that it no longer provides signal. I removed it from loops this month. I have a spicy, optimistic take - I think there's an opportunity for junior engineers: https://felixrieseberg.com/hunge…

Banger report from Google. They just released EmbeddingGemma 2, an open 744M multimodal embedding model. It beats specialist models and models 2 to 12 times larger across seven benchmark suites covering text, code, images, video, documents, and audio. Text, images, audio, video, and mixed inputs all go into one vector space. Each modality has its own encoder feeding into a shared backbone, so you can load only what you need. Text-only runs at 271M parameters, vision-language at 439M, and audio-language at 577M. It scores 61.36 on MTEB Multilingual v2 and 68.46 on MTEB English v2. The int4 version loses about 0.4 points on MTEB Multilingual. You can also lower the vision token budget and truncate the embedding dimensions. For agent memory and retrieval over mixed media, this small open model is a great on-device option. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37364 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/embeddinggemma-2-unified-and-efficient-multimodal-representations-2610.37364

Great paper from Amazon and colleagues on self-improving multi-agent systems. Episodic memory for agents is so underrated. But I am starting to see lots of good applications as frontier models improve. This paper is the latest example. They built a system that has three parts, all run by the same LLM. A controller plans each task and runs it one step at a time, choosing which sub-agent and which skills to use at each step. Sub-agents start as a generalist, and each specialist inherits the generalist's prompt plus its own role-specific method. Skills are short procedures, such as algorithms or pitfall checklists. EMMA treats the controller's routing memory, the agent prompts, and the skills as episodic memory that improves from failures. After a failed task, a reflector decides which of the three owns the fix and proposes one edit there. Guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental, and bounded. EMMA beats ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS, and ADAS on KramaBench, AppWorld, and BBEH, by up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, and uses 17 to 38% fewer training executions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35966 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/emma-structured-episodic-memory-for-multi-agent-workflow-synthesis-2610.35966

Decision models can also improve your OCR pipelines. You can also use Jev-like models for verification. Here is a great example of this: MiniCPM-OCR from OpenBMB and ModelBest pairs a small open document parser with a second model that scores the reliability of the OCR output. The parser has only 1.3B parameters. It handles Chinese and English documents, including scans, photos, curved pages, and tilted inputs, and it supports key information extraction. The second model, MiniCPM-OCR Jev, checks extracted text, formulas, and tables. It also works on outputs from other OCR models, so you can run it on top of the parser you already use. More details below. Agents now read PDFs, invoices, and papers all day. One bad table extraction carries into every step that follows. A simple setup looks like this. > Parse the document with MiniCPM-OCR > Score the extracted text, formulas, and tables with Jev > Send low-scoring output to a human or a correction step Jev estimates reliability. It doesn't fix errors itself. The weights are open, with a fine-tuning framework and inference support for llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang, and Ollama. There are also Agent Skills integrations. If you build document agents, test the parser and Jev together on your hardest pages, like dense tables, formulas, and phone photos. Media

Super interesting paper from Google DeepMind and Stanford. They find that if you put a picture of a red heart in the context, Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.4 write recursive code 100% of the time. They found this on inorder binary tree traversal, a problem with equally valid recursive and iterative solutions. A yellow checkmark pushes Gemini 3.1 Pro to recursion in 90% of samples. The effect matches or comes close to telling the model directly to use recursion. Text captions of the same symbol steer much less, and random or naturalistic images steer less still. The models cannot explain it. Their interpretations of the symbol and their thinking traces do not match what they do. For GPT-5.4, 74.7% of traces give the wrong reason. When models send images to each other, they pick shapes that they and humans find intuitive, and those shapes often fail to steer the other model. If your agents read screenshots or images, those inputs can change behavior in ways the reasoning trace will not show. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36449 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/a-heart-means-recursion-exploring-visual-meaning-and-communication-in-vlms-2610.36449
